intro: Gynaecology covers abnormal bleeding, acute and chronic pelvic pain, endometriosis, PCOS and amenorrhoea, menopause and pelvic floor disorders. These are among the commonest reasons Australian women see a GP, and the AMC tests safe first steps (always the pregnancy test), Australian first-line treatments such as the levonorgestrel IUD, and not missing torsion, PID or endometrial pathology.

lessons.title: Abnormal uterine bleeding and fibroids
objectives: Work up abnormal uterine bleeding with a pregnancy test, FBC, ferritin and the PALM-COEIN framework
Decide who needs pelvic ultrasound and who needs endometrial sampling
Choose Australian first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding, including the levonorgestrel IUD
Recognise fibroid presentations and the options for treating them

sections.heading: What counts as abnormal bleeding
sections.body:
Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is bleeding that is abnormal in **frequency, regularity, duration or volume**, or that occurs between periods, after sex or after menopause. **Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB)** is defined by its impact: excessive menstrual blood loss that interferes with a woman's physical, social, emotional or material quality of life. Nobody measures millilitres in practice; flooding, clots bigger than a 50-cent coin, changing pads overnight, needing double protection and missing work or school are the clues.

HMB is one of the most common reasons women see a GP in Australia and a major cause of **iron deficiency**, which is often missed. The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care's **Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Clinical Care Standard** sets the expected pathway: take a proper history, check iron, use transvaginal ultrasound as first-line imaging, offer the **levonorgestrel IUD** early, and avoid dilatation and curettage (D&C) as a stand-alone diagnostic test.

Postmenopausal bleeding is a separate pathway (endometrial cancer until proven otherwise) and is covered in the gynae-oncology course.

sections.heading: PALM-COEIN: structural versus non-structural
sections.body:
The FIGO **PALM-COEIN** system sorts causes in reproductive-age, non-pregnant women. Learn it as two halves.

| Structural (PALM): seen on imaging or histology | Non-structural (COEIN) |
|---|---|
| **P**olyp (endometrial or cervical) | **C**oagulopathy (von Willebrand disease is the classic) |
| **A**denomyosis | **O**vulatory dysfunction (PCOS, thyroid, prolactin, extremes of reproductive age) |
| **L**eiomyoma (fibroid), especially submucosal | **E**ndometrial (primary disorder of local haemostasis) |
| **M**alignancy and hyperplasia | **I**atrogenic (anticoagulants, hormonal contraception, IUD, SSRIs) |
| | **N**ot yet classified (e.g. AV malformation, niche after caesarean) |

Why this matters mechanically: **anovulatory** cycles mean oestrogen stimulates the endometrium without progesterone to stabilise it, so it breaks down irregularly and unpredictably, often heavily. That is why irregular heavy bleeding clusters at menarche and in perimenopause, and why unopposed oestrogen over years causes hyperplasia. **Ovulatory** HMB with regular cycles is more often structural (fibroid, adenomyosis) or endometrial or a bleeding disorder.

**Fibroids** (leiomyomas) are benign, oestrogen- and progesterone-sensitive smooth-muscle tumours, present in a large proportion of women by 50 and more common in women of African descent. Location drives symptoms: **submucosal** fibroids distort the cavity and cause HMB and subfertility; **intramural** ones enlarge the uterus; **subserosal** and pedunculated ones cause pressure symptoms or, rarely, torsion.

sections.heading: History and examination
sections.body:
- **Pattern:** cycle length, regularity, duration, flooding, clots, intermenstrual (IMB) or postcoital bleeding (PCB). IMB and PCB point to the cervix or cavity (polyp, ectropion, cervicitis, cancer).
- **Impact and anaemia:** fatigue, breathlessness, pica, restless legs.
- **Bleeding disorder screen:** HMB since menarche, bleeding after dental extraction or surgery, postpartum haemorrhage, easy bruising, family history. Suspect von Willebrand disease in a teenager with HMB from the first period.
- **Ovulatory clues:** irregular cycles, acne, hirsutism, weight change, galactorrhoea, thyroid symptoms.
- **Contraception, pregnancy intention, medicines** (anticoagulants, hormonal methods), cervical screening status and STI risk.
- **Pressure symptoms** from fibroids: urinary frequency, constipation, a palpable abdominal mass.

Examination: pallor, BMI, signs of hyperandrogenism or thyroid disease; abdominal palpation; speculum (polyp, cervical lesion, discharge); bimanual (bulky irregular uterus suggests fibroids; a uniformly enlarged, tender, "boggy" uterus suggests adenomyosis). An adolescent with HMB who has never been sexually active does not need a speculum.

sections.heading: What to order and why
sections.body:
1. **Pregnancy test (urine or serum beta-hCG) in every woman of reproductive age.** Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy masquerade as "a heavy period". This is the most tested first step.
2. **FBC and ferritin.** Ferritin is the best test of iron stores; a ferritin below about 30 microgram/L indicates iron deficiency even with a normal haemoglobin.
3. **Chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT** if IMB, PCB or STI risk; **cervical screening** if due (a symptomatic woman with PCB needs a co-test and examination, not a routine screen).
4. **TSH and prolactin** only when the history suggests ovulatory dysfunction; **coagulation studies and von Willebrand screen** when the bleeding history is positive or HMB began at menarche.
5. **Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound** (first-line imaging) when the uterus is enlarged or irregular, symptoms persist despite treatment, or there are risk factors. Saline infusion sonography or **hysteroscopy** evaluates the cavity for polyps and submucosal fibroids.
6. **Endometrial sampling** (Pipelle in clinic, or hysteroscopy with directed biopsy) if the woman is **45 or older** with persistent AUB, or younger with risk factors for hyperplasia: obesity, PCOS with infrequent periods, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome, or failed medical treatment. Blind D&C alone misses focal lesions and is no longer recommended as a diagnostic test.

sections.heading: Treating heavy menstrual bleeding and fibroids
sections.body:
Treat iron deficiency alongside the bleeding (oral iron; IV iron such as ferric carboxymaltose if intolerant, severe or time-critical).

**Medical options for HMB** (choice depends on contraceptive wishes and preference):

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD** | Most effective medical treatment; reduces loss by around 90% over months; also contraception. Offer early. |
| **Tranexamic acid** | Antifibrinolytic, taken only during heavy days; non-hormonal, fine when trying to conceive. Avoid with history of VTE. |
| **NSAIDs** (mefenamic acid, naproxen) | During periods; reduce loss by about a quarter to a third and help dysmenorrhoea. |
| **Combined hormonal contraception** | Regulates and lightens cycles; check UKMEC eligibility. |
| **Progestogens** | Cyclical or continuous oral norethisterone or medroxyprogesterone, DMPA, implant (the implant often gives unpredictable bleeding). |

**Acute heavy bleeding** with haemodynamic compromise: resuscitate, check Hb and group and hold, and use high-dose progestogen or tranexamic acid under specialist advice; admit if unstable.

**Surgical:** polypectomy and resection of submucosal fibroids hysteroscopically; **endometrial ablation** (only when family is complete, and contraception is still needed afterwards); hysterectomy as the definitive option.

**Fibroids:** asymptomatic fibroids need no treatment. For symptoms: the medical HMB options above (the LNG-IUD works best when the cavity is not distorted); **GnRH agonists** shrink fibroids temporarily before surgery but cause menopausal symptoms and bone loss, so they are short-term; **myomectomy** if fertility is desired; **uterine artery embolisation**; hysterectomy. Fibroids shrink after menopause, so a *growing* fibroid in a postmenopausal woman raises concern for leiomyosarcoma. In pregnancy, **red degeneration** causes acute localised pain and tenderness, managed with analgesia.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks it
sections.body:
- "First step" in any reproductive-age woman with bleeding: **pregnancy test**.
- A teenager with HMB since menarche and nosebleeds: **von Willebrand disease**, not a hormone problem.
- "Most effective long-term medical treatment" for HMB in a woman wanting contraception: **LNG-IUD**. Wanting to conceive: **tranexamic acid** (with or without an NSAID).
- A woman in her late 40s with persistent irregular bleeding: ultrasound plus **endometrial sampling**, not reassurance and the pill.
- Fatigue with normal Hb and heavy periods: check **ferritin**.
- Avoid options that describe D&C as the diagnostic test.

keyPoints: Every reproductive-age woman with abnormal bleeding needs a pregnancy test first.
PALM-COEIN splits causes into structural (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy) and non-structural (coagulopathy, ovulatory, endometrial, iatrogenic, not classified).
Check FBC and ferritin; iron deficiency is common and under-treated.
Transvaginal ultrasound is first-line imaging; hysteroscopy with biopsy beats blind D&C.
Endometrial sampling if 45 or over with persistent AUB, or younger with risk factors for hyperplasia.
The levonorgestrel IUD is the most effective medical treatment for HMB.
Tranexamic acid and NSAIDs are non-hormonal options taken only during menstruation.
redFlags: Positive pregnancy test with bleeding or pain (exclude ectopic pregnancy)
Haemodynamic instability or Hb falling with acute heavy bleeding
Postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding with a visible cervical lesion
Persistent AUB in a woman 45 or older, or with obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen or Lynch syndrome
Rapidly enlarging fibroid, especially after menopause

contrast.india: D&C is often used as both diagnosis and treatment for heavy bleeding.
contrast.australia: Transvaginal ultrasound first, then Pipelle or hysteroscopy with directed biopsy. D&C alone is discouraged by the national HMB Clinical Care Standard.

contrast.india: Oral progestogens (norethisterone) and hysterectomy are frequent choices.
contrast.australia: The levonorgestrel IUD is promoted as first-line medical treatment, with tranexamic acid or NSAIDs for those not wanting hormones.
